title: GTA VI was built by hand. The man who ran Take-Two during GTA IV says AI could let a filmmaker make the next breakout game
summary: Take-Two says generative AI played no part in GTA VI. Ben Feder says AI will soon let new creators build games with a point and a click.
content: Grand Theft Auto VI , on track to be the biggest entertainment launch of any kind, was made the old-fashioned way: Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick said in February that Rockstar Games built the game without generative AI. “With regards to GTA 6, generative AI has zero part in what Rockstar Games is building. Their worlds are handcrafted. That’s what differentiates them,” Zelnick told GamesIndustry.biz . “They’re built from the ground up, building by building, street by street, neighborhood by neighborhood.” That’s not to say it didn’t take time and money. Analysts estimate Take-Two spent more than a billion dollars on the game, which came out more than 13 years after its predecessor (Zelnick never confirmed the amount but admitted the game was “expensive”). But the next blockbuster video game might come sooner, cheaper—and with an even more cinematic lens, according to Ben Feder, who ran Take-Two Interactive when Grand Theft Auto IV came out in 2008 . “Some great creative mind who would have otherwise gone to make a film will make a video game because it’s as simple as point and click,” Feder said in a long and winding conversation with Fortune about the state of the entertainment industry. Feder, now managing partner of Tirta Ventures, said in a Fortune commentary this month that AI will change how big games get made. His firm invests in AI-native game projects . “We put our money where our mouth is,” he said of Tirta’s investments. Ben Feder, managing partner at Tirta Ventures and former CEO of Take-Two Interactive. Courtesy of Ben Feder The next great video game maker might be someone who would otherwise have gone into movies, and that’s because AI would make it easier for a filmmaker without a technical background to get into video games. And Feder doesn’t expect that shift to hurt the franchise he once oversaw. “I don’t think GTA is going anywhere. In fact, it probably goes from strength to strength,” Feder said. “But that’s not to say it’s going to get created in the exact same way that it got created here.” Video games have long sat at the intersection of the software and entertainment businesses. Feder said AI will shrink the software side as writing code gets cheaper and easier. “The argument would be that because AI is making software development commoditized, and software points to zero, it becomes much more about entertainment than it does about both entertainment and computer science,” he said. Feder described the result as “somewhere between democratizing creativity—the cynic would say commoditizing creativity—but I don’t believe that creativity, true creativity, really gets commoditized unless you’re such a believer in AI that you think AI can also be creative.” A 13-year ROI More games won’t mean more hits. Feder expects a flood of new titles, with only a small share breaking through, and pointed to YouTube. “I don’t know how many billions of minutes of video have been on YouTube, but how many of them actually are good? How many of them actually get traction?” he said. “But the ones that do get traction and are good reach billions of people, literally, and can create enormous outcomes, both creatively and commercially.” Grand Theft Auto VI shows how large those outcomes can be . Take-Two has not disclosed the game’s cost, though estimates put its development budget at $1 billion to $1.5 billion . Brokerage Oppenheimer projected about $1.85 billion in gross revenue in the game’s first three days, Reuters reported . “Thirteen years of investment you make back in a day. Unbelievable,” Feder said. “But it only happens if you create the most awesome game ever.” AI tools could change that math across the industry, he said. “It’s going to get harder to justify a $2 billion game in a world where the next best alternative is two orders of magnitude less.” GTA VI, ironically, did make back all the money poured into it, and then some. Feder said that counterargument is a pretty good devil’s advocate. “What’s the argument for not spending another $2 billion on the next one and making it back in a day?” he said. “That’s a valid argument.” At this point, the conversation focused on the lived experience of the entertainment industry at large. While most people think of film and cinema as making up the lion’s share of what people consider entertainment, video games have always been there, and they’ve been blockbusters of their own. But recently, as with movies, it seems big publishers have long concentrated their money on a handful of games, or, as the Marvel Cinematic Universe has shown, on the franchise model. “Even when I was at Take-Two for GTA IV, we were the first, and others followed, to develop a strategy of fewer, bigger titles,” Feder said. And just like movies, the indie games have a tough time breaking through the noise. Feder said the pressure falls on games in the middle, those with big budgets and smaller audiences. “It’s hard to make the numbers work.” Feder said that when he ran Take-Two, he saw the industry’s next frontier as characters that look like movie actors rather than figures in a game. Of GTA VI , he said, “This gets as close to it as I’ve ever seen.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: L.A. Lakers announce deal with Kalshi, signaling sports leagues’ growing embrace of prediction markets
summary: The NBA joins other major leagues in welcoming prediction markets, while the NFL pushes in the opposite direction.
content: The Los Angeles Lakers have announced a tie-up with Kalshi, becoming the latest sports team to partner with a prediction market—and leaving little doubt about where the National Basketball Association has placed its chips in the ongoing debate about the role of the controversial wagering platforms in the world of pro sports. The team announced the news on Tuesday in a brief statement that hailed the partnership, but offered few details on what it will entail. “We’re excited … to explore innovative ways to engage fans and strengthen their connection to the game,” said Los Angeles Lakers president and chief business officer Lon Rosen. The announcement also solidified a broader alliance between the NBA and prediction markets. The league officially embraced the platforms only a month ago, when it named Kalshi and Polymarket its preferred exchanges. Kalshi has since moved quickly to turn that opening into team-level agreements, signing the Philadelphia 76ers in October before adding the Lakers this week. The NBA’s overall positioning came as something of a surprise, given that it and the National Football League had largely held back while other major sports leagues signed agreements with prediction markets. Some of these platforms let users as young as 18 wager on event contracts, with sports making up the bulk of trading. Other major sports organizations have mostly taken a welcoming approach. The National Hockey League became the first major North American professional sports league to strike prediction market deals in October 2025, signing multiyear agreements with Kalshi and Polymarket that included rights to league data, branding, and broadcast advertising. That push expanded to more teams last week, when seven NHL teams announced their own marketing deals with Novig . Others, including Major League Soccer, Major League Baseball, and UFC, have also struck deals with prediction markets. The NFL, meanwhile, has remained as the odd one out. In early October, the league filed a 24-page brief urging the Supreme Court to back state gambling regulators, who argue that sports prediction contracts should follow the same rules as traditional sports bets. At the heart of that dispute is whether the contracts are financial products governed by federal regulators or bets subject to state gambling laws. The league also raised concerns about cheating, insider trading , consumer protection, and risks to younger users. The legal fight also hangs over the Lakers’ new partnership. California allows tribal casinos and a state lottery, but it has kept traditional sports betting off the table, with a bookmaking ban dating back more than a century. The state kept that prohibition in place after the Supreme Court cleared the way for states to legalize sports betting in 2018, and voters rejected two legalization measures in 2022. If the Supreme Court takes up the case and sides with state regulators, Kalshi could face new limits on offering sports contracts in California—complicating its push to reach fans in the Lakers’ home market. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: After $26 billion in gifts, MacKenzie Scott is still worth $27 billion—and just gave Atlanta students $8 million more
summary: Her second $8 million gift to Achieve Atlanta lands as Amazon, now No. 1 on the Fortune 500, keeps her net worth above $27 billion.
content: Four years ago, MacKenzie Scott gave $8 million to Achieve Atlanta, a nonprofit that helps Atlanta public school students pay for and finish college. Last week, the organization announced she had done it again , with a second $8 million gift that brings her total support to $16 million. It is one of two gifts Scott made to Georgia education nonprofits this month, together worth $12.5 million. The donor has given away more than $26 billion since her 2019 divorce from Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, yet is still worth more than $27 billion, largely because Amazon stock keeps rising. For an Atlanta Public Schools graduate pursuing a bachelor’s degree, the need-based Achieve Atlanta scholarship can be worth up to $20,000 over four years . Students at two-year colleges and in technical programs can receive $1,500 a year for up to four semesters. The nonprofit also helps students choose colleges, work through the application process, and find their first jobs. Since 2015, it has awarded more than $75 million in scholarships. An independent evaluation by researchers affiliated with Georgia State University’s Georgia Policy Labs found that 91% of Achieve Atlanta scholars returned for a second semester of college. Among peers who also graduated from Atlanta Public Schools, had similar academic and demographic backgrounds, and enrolled in college without the program’s support, 77% did. The gap narrows over time but holds. Six years after high school, 42% of scholars had graduated, compared with 36% of similar peers. “The repeated investment by Scott is a testament to the success of Achieve Atlanta’s postsecondary success model,” the nonprofit said in announcing the gift. Scott’s latest giving in Georgia also supports women returning to school later in life. The Athens-based Jeannette Rankin Foundation received $4.5 million, its largest single donation to date, according to The Atlanta Journal-Constitution . Karen Sterk, the foundation’s CEO, told the newspaper that its support could benefit more than a million women. The two gifts fit a pattern. Scott’s higher education giving has largely bypassed elite universities in favor of HBCUs, community colleges, and tribal colleges , and her giving to historically Black colleges and universities alone has topped $1 billion , Fortune has reported. How Scott’s fortune held up as she gave it away When Scott and Bezos finalized their divorce in July 2019 after 25 years of marriage, she received roughly 4% of Amazon. The shares were worth about $37 billion then . Since then, she has given away more than $26 billion through more than 2,700 gifts to nonprofits, according to Yield Giving, the organization she set up to make them. Forbes still estimates her net worth is more than $27 billion. Her stake has shrunk. In the year through September 2025, Scott cut her Amazon holdings by 42% , according to a regulatory filing that did not say whether she sold, donated, or both. But the shares she kept have kept climbing. Amazon stock gained more than 42% over the five years through July 2026, as Fortune previously reported . Those gains help explain why Scott is still worth tens of billions of dollars even as she gives away much of her fortune. The company behind that fortune is now the largest in the U.S. by revenue. Amazon ranks No. 1 on the 2026 Fortune 500 , ending Walmart’s 13-year run at the top. Scott signed the Giving Pledge in 2019, committing to give away the majority of her wealth during her lifetime or in her will. Her largest gifts include $436 million to Habitat for Humanity , $281 million to Boys & Girls Clubs of America , and $275 million to Planned Parenthood . What she wants her money to do before she gives it away Scott has also described what she wants her money to do while she still owns it. In a 2024 essay , she wrote that she asked her investment team to find funds and companies working on the same problems she supports through philanthropy. Her examples included affordable housing funds and digital health platforms for women. When she makes a gift, she wrote, she would rather draw the money from those investments than from a stock portfolio “that increases the wealth and influence of leaders who already have it.” She wants to back ventures led by people from the communities they serve, or by founders who often struggle to raise capital, including women and people of color. Her idea was that the same dollar could help twice: first as an investment in those ventures, and later as a donation to a nonprofit. As Scott wrote in her Giving Pledge letter, “It will take time and effort and care. But I won’t wait. And I will keep at it until the safe is empty.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: The AI boom helped lift retirement accounts, but the Nvidia whiplash showed how much investors’ financial futures depend on a handful of stocks
summary: Ten stocks make up 39% of the S&P 500, and nearly two-thirds of Fidelity 401(k) savers keep everything in a target-date fund.
content: Millions of Americans, and their financial futures, may be exposed to the recent AI-fueled swings in the market regardless of whether they’ve ever used a chatbot. Stocks plunged Wednesday morning before recovering much of the loss. Near the start of trading, the Dow fell more than 1,000 points and the Nasdaq dropped more than 4% as AI chip stocks sold off for a second straight day. Nvidia fell as much as 8%. By late afternoon, the S&P 500 had cut its loss to about half a percent, and the Dow had turned higher. Wednesday’s swing capped a week in which a single company’s board decision moved the index that holds much of Americans’ retirement accounts. Roughly two-thirds of of Fidelity 401(k) savers keep everything in a target-date fund. Following a tumultuous few weeks in which Jensen Huang resigned and was later reinstated as CEO of Nvidia, the chipmaker’s stock jumped 31%, added about $950 billion in market value, and lifted the S&P 500 by 4.7%. Still, the S&P 500 is now about 8% below its Oct. 6 record. Last Friday it closed 11.6% below that high, putting it in correction territory, after seven straight losses, its longest losing streak since February 2020. Stock market concentration has been on the rise for years, and it is now near 35-year highs. Just 10 stocks in the S&P 500 account for about 39% of its total market capitalization, with the five largest stocks—all tech giants—alone accounting for 29%, according to Charles Schwab . That means an American with $100,000 in an index fund tied to the S&P 500 would have $29,000 in just five stocks. As a result, many investors may think they are putting money into a diversified investment when the health of their portfolios may actually be tied more to the fate of a handful of tech giants than they realize, said Martin Mulyadi, a professor of accounting at Shenandoah University’s College of Business, Engineering & Technology. “An index fund spreads your money across 500 companies, but it does not spread the risk evenly,” he told Fortune . For the millions of Americans who have poured their money into S&P 500 index funds through their 401(k)s, this concentration has been a boon in recent years. A booming stock market that has risen just over 50% during the past five years helped push the number of 401(k) millionaires at Fidelity to a record 769,000 in June . Even before the selloff began, that number had fallen some 2% between the second and third quarters, but was still up 15% from a year earlier, according to Fidelity. Through the third quarter, the vast majority of retirement savers were still investing. About 96% of 401(k) participants at Fidelity either maintained or increased their savings rate during the third quarter, the financial services company revealed in a report this week. “Despite market volatility, many workers continue to increase their savings, stay invested, and take advantage of workplace retirement plan features designed to support long-term success,” Sharon Brovelli, Fidelity’s president of workplace investing, said in a statement. Yet the growing dominance of a handful of technology giants means even those who have followed conventional retirement wisdom and have added to diversified funds may be exposed to heightened risk. A further stock slide could hurt the portfolios of millions of Americans and especially for those closer to retirement: The average Fidelity 401(k) millionaire is 58 years old. Retirement at risk For older Americans, a downturn early in retirement could have implications for when they can afford to stop working and how much money they’ll have to live on once they do. By selling investments at depressed prices to cover living expenses, retirees face the problem of sequence-of-returns risk . If a falling stock market in early retirement causes retirees to sell their investments at lower prices, that means they have less money left in the market that could later benefit from an eventual recovery. To try to avoid this phenomenon, Charles Schwab recommends maintaining a short-term reserve of low-risk and more liquid investments that retirees could draw from in a downturn to avoid touching their portfolio. The increasing concentration of the stock market also doesn’t necessarily mean investors should abandon index funds altogether. Investors should instead consider taking a closer look at the makeup of their portfolio, said Sean McEvilly, the managing partner and founder of Vistamark Investments. “The practical move isn’t to bail out of stocks. It’s to look at the whole 401(k), since target-date and large-cap funds often hold the same names, and make sure there’s real exposure to small and midsized companies, international stocks, and bonds,” McEvilly told Fortune . This story was originally featured on Fortune.com
